passages.t: Children and parents, in the Lord
passages.happening:
The household passage goes on. Paul speaks to the children in the church: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (verse 1).

He quotes the commandment: “‘Honor your father and mother’ (which is the first commandment with a promise), ‘that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth’” (verses 2-3).

Then he speaks to fathers: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The first thing to notice is that Paul speaks to children at all. The letter was read aloud in church, and the children were there listening. Paul treats them as real members of the church, who can hear God's word and answer to the Lord for themselves.

‘In the Lord’ matters. Children obey their parents as part of following Jesus. Their obedience belongs to him first.

In a Roman household the father held legal power over his children for as long as he lived, and harsh discipline was common. Ordinary advice about running a household told fathers how to rule. Paul tells them what not to do: do not provoke your children to anger. That puts a limit on a father's power that the world around him did not.

‘Discipline and instruction’ means the whole upbringing of a child: teaching, training and correction. And it is ‘of the Lord’. Parents are not raising children to fit their own pride or plans. They are raising them for God, and their way of doing it should look like his: patient, truthful and kind.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes the fifth commandment. “Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12). His wording, ‘that it may go well with you’, comes from the form in Deuteronomy: “so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you” (Deuteronomy 5:16). The promise of the land becomes a promise of life ‘on the earth’.

Israel's parents were told to teach their children God's ways in the middle of ordinary life: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

Proverbs gives both parents a voice: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother” (Proverbs 1:8). And the Psalms call children a gift: “Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD” (Psalm 127:3).
passages.hard:
Does ‘obey your parents’ mean a child must obey whatever a parent says? No. Paul says ‘in the Lord’. A child's obedience belongs to Christ first, and no parent can command what Christ forbids. And in the very next verse Paul limits the parent: do not provoke your children to anger. These verses describe a home where a parent's authority is held under God and used for the child's good.

These words must never be used against a child who is being harmed. No one may use ‘obey your parents’ to keep a child quiet about abuse, or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: If you are young, ask what it would look like to honour your parents this week, in the Lord. If you are a parent, ask what in your home provokes your children to anger: harshness, unfairness, broken promises, or never having time. Ask whether your children see in you the patience and kindness of the Lord you are teaching them about.

passages.t: Slaves and masters under one Master
passages.happening:
Paul speaks to slaves. “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ” (verse 5). Not only when someone is watching, “but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart” (verse 6). “Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free” (verses 7-8).

Then to masters. “And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Slaves worked in houses, fields, mines and workshops; some were trusted managers or teachers, others did crushing labour. People became slaves through war, through being born to an enslaved mother, through debt, or by being abandoned as babies and sold. Roman slavery was not based on race, and many slaves in the cities could hope to be freed one day. But by law a slave was property. A slave could be bought and sold, beaten, separated from family and used sexually by the master.

Many early Christians were slaves, and some were masters, and they sat in the same church and heard this letter read together. So notice what the slaves heard. They were spoken to directly, as people with hearts and wills, not as tools. They were told their work was seen by Christ, and that the Lord would reward them, ‘whether he is slave or free’.

And notice what the masters heard, in front of their own slaves. Stop threatening. You are not the final master here. You have a Master too, and he does not take your side because you are the owner. The word for slave and the word for servant are the same word in Greek. Paul tells both slave and master that they belong to Christ.
passages.ot:
The God of Israel shows no favouritism: “For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17).

Job says why he could not mistreat his own servants: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

Israel's law told masters, “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43), and reminded them, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 15:15). It made kidnapping a person a capital crime (Exodus 21:16), and said, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15).
passages.hard:
Why does Paul tell slaves to obey instead of condemning slavery? Paul does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence.

But within that world he does what ordinary household rules did not. He speaks to slaves as people who answer to God. He tells masters to give up threats. He puts master and slave under one Lord, with no favouritism. Elsewhere, on the most common reading of a debated verse, he tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he asks Philemon to take back Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). Many readers see in this the seeds of the truth that would undo slavery: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The history of these verses is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used Ephesians 6:5 to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the words to masters and the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

Nor are these verses a simple rule for employment today. A worker is not property, and a boss is not an owner. Some of what Paul says, to work honestly and to treat workers without threats, can be applied to work with care. But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.

The Honest Answer ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’ goes further.
passages.asks: Paul tells everyone in the house that they answer to the same Lord. Ask whom you treat as beneath you, at work, at home or in church. If you have power over others, ask whether you use threats, open or quiet. And ask whether you see the people who serve you as Christ sees them.

passages.t: The armour of God, and prayer
passages.happening:
“Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (verses 10-11).

Paul says who the real enemy is: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (verse 12).

Then the armour, piece by piece: “the belt of truth buckled around your waist”, “the breastplate of righteousness”, feet “fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace”, “the shield of faith”, “the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (verses 14-17).

And last, prayer: “Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition” (verse 18). Paul asks them to pray for him, that he will speak boldly, “for which I am an ambassador in chains” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
Paul wrote as a prisoner, and may have been chained to a Roman guard. His readers knew Roman armour well: a belt, a breastplate, boots, a large shield, a helmet and a short sword. But every piece he names is a gift of God: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and God's word.

Notice the word ‘stand’. It comes again and again. Most of this armour is for standing firm, not for attacking. Only the sword strikes, and the sword is the word of God. The victory has already been won by Christ (1:20-22). Believers hold the ground he has taken.

The ‘struggle’ is a word from wrestling, a close fight. And Paul says plainly who it is against: not ‘flesh and blood’, not human beings. Other people, even those who oppose or hurt us, are not the enemy in this fight. The enemy is the evil behind the world's darkness.

Then comes prayer, which holds it all together. Notice that the great apostle asks for prayer. He does not ask to be set free. He asks for courage to speak. An ‘ambassador’ speaks for a king, and Paul speaks for his King even in chains.
passages.ot:
The armour is God's own, taken from Isaiah. There God sees that no one will save his people, and puts on armour himself: “He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head” (Isaiah 59:17).

Of the coming King, Isaiah says, “Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist” (Isaiah 11:5). Paul's belt is truth.

The feet ready with the gospel of peace recall Isaiah 52:7: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace”.

The sword of the Spirit, the word of God, recalls the Servant who says, “He made My mouth like a sharp sword” (Isaiah 49:2), and the King who “will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth” (Isaiah 11:4).

The shield has no single source in Isaiah, but God's people had long called God himself their shield: “The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him” (Psalm 28:7).
passages.hard:
Paul uses the language of battle. Does this give Christians a reason to fight other people?

No. Paul says it plainly: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (verse 12). The armour is for standing against evil, not for attacking neighbours, opponents or other nations. Its pieces are truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation, God's word and prayer. Its one sword is the word of God, and even the shoes are the gospel of peace. Elsewhere Paul says, “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

These verses have sometimes been used to turn people into enemies, to treat a political side, another faith or another country as the forces of darkness. That turns the passage upside down. The cross belongs to no flag, and no nation or party is God's army. The person across the street, or across the world, is someone Christ died for.

Nor should these verses make anyone afraid that every trouble is an attack from evil spirits. Paul says evil is real. He also says Christ is seated far above every power (1:21), and that believers stand in his strength, not their own.
passages.asks: Paul says your struggle is not against flesh and blood. Ask whom you have treated as the enemy, and whether you need to see them again as a person Christ loves. Ask which piece of the armour you most need today. And ask who you could pray for, as Paul asked to be prayed for, that they would have courage.

passages.happening:
Paul ends with news and a blessing. “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing” (verse 21). “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts” (verse 22).

Then the last words: “Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
Tychicus was from the province of Asia and travelled with Paul (Acts 20:4). He carried this letter. In Colossians, almost the same words are used about him, and he travels with Onesimus, the slave Paul wrote to Philemon about (Colossians 4:7-9). So many readers think Ephesians and Colossians were sent at the same time.

Notice how short the ending is. Paul's letters usually close with greetings to many people by name. This one has none. That fits the view that the letter was meant for several churches, not one.

The letter ends as it began, with grace and peace (1:2). Everything between, all the praise and all the commands, sits inside that grace. And the last words are about love: ‘an undying love’ for Jesus. The letter that began by speaking of God's love for us before the world was made ends by speaking of our love for him.
passages.ot: The closing words echo the blessing God gave Israel's priests to speak over the people: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26). Grace and peace were God's gifts to Israel long before Paul wrote them at the end of a letter.
passages.asks: Tychicus was sent to ‘encourage your hearts’. Ask who needs that from you this week, and what you could do or say. And as the letter ends, ask whether your love for Jesus is the kind that lasts: not only warm on a good day, but steady through hard ones.
